translations.text: "Beat your sickles into swords and your pruning hooks into spears; let the weak say: I am mighty."

The image here depicts the gathering of the nations for war under divine judgment, then announces that the final battle is not outside the domain of God's authority. Thus the book uses the language of war to proclaim the end of the rebellion of the nations before God's judgment.
32. "The Lord is a refuge for His people"
After the announcement of judgment comes a promise of utmost importance:
"And the Lord will be a refuge for His people and a fortress for the children of Israel."

And this phrase brings us back to the heart of the book: the God who permitted discipline is Himself the refuge in the end. For the goal is not that man should live in constant fear of God, but that he should learn that the Lord is the true place of safety.
33. "And the Lord will dwell in Zion"
The book closes with the image of the divine presence:
"And the Lord will dwell in Zion."

And this conclusion harmonizes with many of the prophetic books, where redemption reaches its goal when God is in the midst of His people. For the redemption of the land, harvests, and economy is not the true end; the end is the restoration of relationship and divine presence.
34. The most important persons in the book
The prophet who proclaimed the message of repentance, the day of the Lord, the Spirit, and redemption.
Pethuel
The father of Joel, the only person explicitly mentioned as the father of the prophet.
They were an essential part of the leadership of the people in fasting, prayer, and calling to repentance.
The elders
Addressed as leaders of the community and bearers of its memory and wisdom.
The children of Israel
The primary audience of the message, and the community that experienced the crisis of the locusts and then was called to repentance and redemption.
Appears at the end of the book as a subject of judgment before the Lord.
35. The most important events in the book

The invasion of the locust upon the land, destruction of harvests, vineyards, and trees, cessation of offering and libation, calling of the priests to fasting, announcement of the approach of the day of the Lord, the call to return with all the heart, the promise of mercy, restoration of the land and harvests, promise of rain, compensation for the years that the locust devoured, the outpouring of the Spirit upon all flesh, the heavenly and earthly prophecies connected with the day of the Lord, the announcement of salvation for those who call upon the name of the Lord, then the judgment of the nations and the establishment of the Lord in Zion.
36. The most important message the book presents

God is able to transform disaster into a call to repentance, repentance into redemption, and redemption into a life in the Spirit, and therefore man should not read crises as mere destruction without meaning; for God calls His people to rend their hearts and not their garments, to return to Him, and then announces that His ultimate goal is not the destruction of His people but their redemption, the outpouring of His Spirit upon them, and making them live in His presence.
37. What does the book of Joel point to us?

The book points first that crises can become a spiritual warning, without this meaning that every specific disaster is a direct punishment for a specific sin. It points second that true repentance is not an external religious display but a returning of the heart to God. It points third that God is able to restore what years of devastation have corrupted, but it also announces that the greatest restoration is the outpouring of the Spirit and life in the presence of God. Finally, the book lifts our eyes to the day of the Lord, where God's justice becomes clear and the salvation of those who call upon His name appears.
38. Joel and the Messiah

Joel is connected to the Messiah in an indirect yet important way through the kingdom of God, salvation, the outpouring of the Holy Spirit, and the day of the Lord. And in the New Testament the promise of Joel two is directly connected to the event of Pentecost that occurred after the ascension of the Messiah, where Peter announced that what is happening is the fulfillment of what Joel said. And thus the Messiah is the One who opens the way in the apostolic proclamation to the stage in which the Spirit is poured out upon believers, and Joel's promise becomes part of the story of salvation that was fulfilled in the Messiah.
39. Joel and the Holy Spirit
If there is one text that the researcher must remember to understand the book of Joel, it is:
"And afterward I will pour out My Spirit upon all flesh."

For the Spirit in Joel is not a secondary idea, but represents the great turning point from mere restoration of the land to the spiritual restoration of man. And therefore Joel two is directly connected to Acts two, and forms one of the most important bridges between the promise of the Old Covenant and the experience of the early church on the day of Pentecost.
40. Joel and the day of the Lord

The "day of the Lord" in Joel carries two interwoven dimensions; it is connected to the historical judgment that the people experienced, and at the same time it transcends it to the final day of judgment. And therefore it should not be reduced to a single event only, because the language of the prophets often makes earlier historical events serve as shadows or preliminaries to God's ultimate acts. And thus the locust becomes a warning picture that leads to a greater vision concerning God's judgment and His salvation at the end of history.
41. Joel and resurrection and judgment

The book does not present a detailed doctrinal explanation of the doctrine of resurrection as we find in Daniel twelve, but it establishes a strong framework for the final judgment of the nations and the day of the Lord. And when that is combined with the New Testament's announcement concerning resurrection and judgment, Joel becomes part of the larger picture that affirms that history has a moral end, and that God will hold evil accountable and declare the salvation of His people.
42. The grand movement of the book of Joel
Destruction.
Warning.
Fasting.
Rending of the heart.
Restoration of the years.
Outpouring of the Spirit.
Judgment of the nations.
"The Lord dwelling in Zion."

And thus the book begins from a land dried up that the locust has eaten and ends with a land in which the presence of the Lord dwells, and between the beginning and the end we find repentance and mercy and the Spirit and restoration.
43. Summary of the book of Joel
Name of the book Joel
The Hebrew יוֹאֵל — Yôʾēl
Meaning of the name The Lord is God
The author Joel son of Pethuel
Date of birth and death not recorded
Time of writing uncertain; subject of scholarly debate
Audience Judah and Jerusalem
The fundamental crisis Plague of locusts
Central theme The day of the Lord and repentance and redemption
Most important call "Return to Me with all your hearts"
Most important promise "I will pour out My Spirit upon all flesh"
Most important prophetic theme The day of the Lord
Most important connection to the New Testament Acts two
The redemptive text "Whoever calls upon the name of the Lord will be saved"
The end Judgment of the nations and the dwelling of the Lord in Zion

The foundational biblical texts: the book of Joel one through three, along with study of Exodus ten to understand the locust in the plagues of Egypt, and Deuteronomy twenty-eight to understand the locust within the curses of the covenant, and Isaiah two and thirteen and thirty-four, and Jeremiah twenty-five, and Ezekiel thirty, and Amos five to understand the concept of the day of the Lord in the prophetic tradition. And in the New Testament one must especially return to Acts two, verses fourteen through twenty-one, and Romans ten, verse thirteen, because Peter and Paul use texts from Joel in proclaiming salvation and the work of the Holy Spirit.
🔑 The sentence that summarizes the book of Joel

"The book of Joel begins with a land devoured by locusts, but it does not allow man to see the destruction without hearing the voice of God; the locust becomes a warning, the warning leads to the day of the Lord, the day of the Lord leads to the rending of the heart and the return, the return opens the door of mercy, mercy restores what the years have devoured, then surpasses the restoration of the land to a greater promise: 'I will pour out My Spirit upon all flesh,' until the book reaches the salvation of those who call upon the name of the Lord and the judgment of the nations and the dwelling of the Lord in Zion; and thus the story of destruction becomes a story of restoration, and the dry land becomes a land that knows the presence of God, and the voice of the whole book becomes one call: Return to the Lord with all your hearts."
The Gospel of John

The name "John" means "the Lord is gracious" or "the Lord shows favor," and it is a common name in the New Testament. And the Gospel is traditionally attributed to John son of Zebedee, one of the twelve and a disciple of the Messiah who was particularly close to Him, and the book presents a profound theological testimony concerning the person of Jesus the Messiah and His divine identity and His saving work.

Christian tradition attributes the Gospel of John to John son of Zebedee, a fisherman of Galilee and one of the sons of Zebedee, whom the Messiah called along with his brother James. And John was in the closest circle around the Messiah, and appeared with Peter and James in important events such as the raising of Jairus's daughter and the Transfiguration and Gethsemane. And the Gospel refers to "the disciple whom Jesus loved" as a witness to the events, and connects this disciple to the testimony upon which the Gospel is based.
3. For whom was the Gospel written?

It appears that John wrote for a broader Christian audience, both Jews and Gentiles, with the goal of confirming faith in the Messiah and revealing His reality clearly. And therefore he does not depend on explaining Jewish details in the same way that we find in Mark, but uses selected events and dialogues to lead the reader to faith that Jesus is the Messiah, the Son of God.
4. The reason for writing the Gospel

John announces his purpose clearly himself at the end of the Gospel: "And these have been written that you may believe that Jesus is the Messiah, the Son of God, and that believing you may have life in His name." Therefore the Gospel is not merely a historical biography of the Messiah, but an intentional testimony that leads to faith and life. John chose a number of signs and works and discourses that reveal the identity of the Messiah and call the reader to take a stance toward Him.
5. The time of writing of the Gospel

Many researchers consider that the Gospel of John was written in the late first century AD, with disagreement in determining the exact date. A large number of studies place it around ninety AD, while there are other views with earlier dates. And the Gospel itself does not provide a definite date for writing, therefore the determination of the year should be treated as a historical estimate, not a clear biblical fact.

The central theme in the Gospel of John is Jesus the Messiah, the Son of God, the eternal Word who became flesh, and who grants eternal life to everyone who believes in Him. And John presents the Messiah as the source of life and light and truth and the way and the resurrection, and constantly leads the reader from the sign to faith, and from faith to life.
7. The eternal Word

John opens his Gospel with one of the deepest theological statements in Scripture: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God." And here John does not begin from Bethlehem, but looks back before creation, to proclaim the eternality of the Messiah and His relationship to the Father and His participation in the divine nature.

Then He says that "the Word became flesh and dwelt among us," and thus John connects the eternality of the Son with the incarnation. For the Messiah who appeared in history is the same eternal Word who was in the beginning.
8. The Messiah and life

Life is one of the central concepts in John; the Messiah is the source of life, and He grants man eternal life that transcends mere continuation of physical existence. This truth appears in His saying: "I am the resurrection and the life," and in His promise that whoever believes in Him will have eternal life.
